title: A hand on Prahlada's head
hookLine: the hands that ended a tyrant rest on a child's head
carry: the fierce god's hand is a blessing
tomorrow: Prahlada's grandson takes heaven. who's the one left crying?

lines: THE HAND NO GOD WOULD APPROACH.
cards: A hand on the top of your head: a parent checking for fever, a grandparent's blessing, a coach after a loss. Go back to the moment Prahlada first bowed.
The Bhagavata says Narasimha laid his hand on the boy's head, the same hand the gods had been too afraid to come near. Now the boy has one wish to spend. He doesn't spend it on himself.
He spends it on his father.

teach.b: His father. The king who tried every way to be rid of him, who struck the pillar to prove his son wrong. Prahlada asks Narasimha to free his father from the wrong he did to his own child.
Not to pretend it didn't happen.

teach.h: NOT ERASED. NOT HELD AGAINST HIM.
teach.b: To let it not stand against him. And Narasimha grants it, saying, in the telling, that the father is made pure because such a son was born in his family. Now come back to the hand.
Raging, Narasimha frightened even the gods. Then a child bowed at his feet, and the Lord lifted him and laid a hand on his head. That's a blessing, and Hindu families still give it the same way.
When a child bows and touches an elder's feet, the elder rests a hand on the child's head and blesses them: ashirvad.

teach.h: A HAND ON THE HEAD: A BLESSING.
teach.b: The fierce hand and the blessing hand are one hand.

Temples show Narasimha both ways: fierce, ugra, in the doorway, and calm, sometimes with the goddess Lakshmi beside him. Devotees keep both, because his fierceness was never aimed at the child. It was protection.
And the blessing ran further than anyone expected: through the boy, to the very father who had harmed him. That's how the Narasimha story closes. Not with claws.
With a hand on a head.

how: When children bow and touch an elder's feet, the elder's hand on the head gives the blessing, ashirvad. Temple images show Narasimha fierce in the doorway or seated in calm, sometimes with Lakshmi beside him, and some families pray to him for protection.

o: a lion-headed guardian set at temple doors
Prahlada's name for his own father, the king
Vishnu as the man-lion, fierce and gentle at once

games.q: fierce and gentle — tap the pairs.

s: Narasimha is only ever pictured in a rage
temple images show him fierce in the doorway and seated in calm too.
Prahlada spends his one wish on his father
he asks that the wrong done to him not stand against his father.
Prahlada's wish pretends the harm never happened
it doesn't erase it; it asks that it not stand against him.

games.q: at a family puja you touch Nani's feet and she rests her hand on your head. a friend asks what that means. by today's story?
o: it's a blessing, ashirvad, like Narasimha's hand on Prahlada's head.
it just shows the elder outranks you; nothing more.
it means you did something wrong and she's forgiving you.
games.why: the fierce Lord lifted the bowing child and laid a hand on his head. families still bless the same way.

practice: Rest one palm lightly on the top of your head, the way an elder gives a blessing, and breathe slowly under it. If you pray, ask a blessing for someone who has been hard on you, the way Prahlada did for his father.
If you don't, simply hold that person in mind, kindly, for a few breaths. And next time you greet an elder, notice the hand.

wordCard.voice: Narasimha: the man-lion, fierce toward harm, whose hand on Prahlada's head was a blessing.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the man-lion. Fierce in the doorway, calm as he blesses the boy.

carryVoice: The line: the fierce god's hand is a blessing, and Prahlada spent his one wish on his father. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 7.9 (Prahlada bows; Narasimha places his hand on the boy's head)
Bhagavata Purana 7.10.15–19 (Prahlada asks that his father be freed from the sin against him; Narasimha: he is purified because such a son was born in his family)
